Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] External Microsoft Teams chat/call from unfamiliar tenant impersonating IT/helpdesk · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake IT support calls on Microsoft Teams push EtherRAT malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Msiexec installing remote EtherRAT loader MSI (v#.msi) from camorreado.click · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Dual remote-access tools (HopToDesk + AnyDesk) installed on same host within short window · [LLM] Endpoint DNS/network egress to EtherRAT delivery & C2 domain camorreado.click · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
External Microsoft Teams chat/call from unfamiliar tenant impersonating IT/helpdesk AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound Microsoft Teams external-access chat/message activity from a foreign M365 tenant whose account poses as IT support (e.g. helpdesk@Progressive936.onmicrosoft.com). This is the initial-access lure in the EtherRAT vishing campaign where the 'External unfamiliar' Teams contact precedes a remote-control request. Rationale: Anchors on the article's concrete external-tenant IOC (helpdesk@Progressive936.onmicrosoft.com) plus the 'External unfamiliar' impersonation pattern; ExternalAccess==true on Teams from an onmicrosoft.com sender posing as helpdesk is the campaign's exact entry signal. Datadog/Falcon left empty — Teams audit isn't in FDR or Datadog's listed Azure sources. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/18/crosstenant-helpdesk-impersonation-data-exfiltration-human-operated-intrusion-playbook/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/10/07/disrupting-threats-targeting-microsoft-teams/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1656
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate managed-service-provider (MSP) helpdesk that operates from its own M365 tenant and contacts staff via external Teams
  • Partner/vendor IT collaborating cross-tenant during a genuine support case
  • Internal 'helpdesk' shared mailbox federated as a guest in a subsidiary tenant
  • Approved outsourced service-desk display names containing 'IT Support'
Suppression filter
| where UPN !has_any ("contoso-msp", "trusted-partner")  // append approved partner onmicrosoft tenants
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the sender tenant (onmicrosoft.com domain) is not an approved partner; check whether the recipient accepted a screen-share/remote-control request in the same Teams session and whether any download followed. Step 2 (contain): Block the external tenant/domain in Teams external-access policy, disable the impacted user's active sessions, and quarantine the endpoint if remote-control was granted. Step 3 (hunt): On the recipient's device pivot to RMM installs (hoptodesk.exe/anydesk.exe) and msiexec pulling from camorreado.click within the following hour.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application =~ "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType in~ ("ChatCreated","MemberAdded","MessageSent","MessagesListed")
| extend UPN = tostring(RawEventData.UserId)
| where UPN has "onmicrosoft.com"
| where UPN has "Progressive936" or tolower(AccountDisplayName) has_any ("helpdesk","help desk","it support","system administrator") or tolower(UPN) has "helpdesk"
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, UPN, IPAddress, AccountType, ObjectName
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload =~ "MicrosoftTeams"
| where ExternalAccess == true
| where Operation in~ ("ChatCreated","MemberAdded","MessageSent","MessagesExported")
| where UserId has "onmicrosoft.com"
| where UserId has "Progressive936" or tolower(UserId) has "helpdesk" or tolower(UserId) has "it-support"
| project TimeGenerated, Operation, UserId, ClientIP, UserAgent, OfficeId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity` Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation IN ("ChatCreated","MemberAdded","MessageSent") ExternalAccess=true
| search (UserId="*Progressive936*" OR UserId="*helpdesk*" OR UserId="*it-support*" OR UserId="*helpdesk@*.onmicrosoft.com")
| stats min(_time) as firstSeen, count, values(Operation) as operations, values(ClientIP) as srcIPs by UserId
| sort - firstSeen
Dual remote-access tools (HopToDesk + AnyDesk) installed on same host within short window AICommand & Control High
Hunts a host that executes BOTH HopToDesk and AnyDesk within a short window — the exact dual-RMM staging the attacker walks the victim through after the Teams remote-control grant. Two distinct remote-access tools appearing together on one endpoint is far higher fidelity than either tool alone. Rationale: Uses the two specific RMM binaries named in the article (HopToDesk, AnyDesk) and requires BOTH on the same host — the dcount>=2 requirement suppresses the common single-legit-AnyDesk noise while capturing the attacker's exact staging step. Datadog rule groups by host and thresholds distinctTools at rule level. Cross-checked against: • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2026/06/inside-a-malicious-infrastructure-delivering-etherrat-phishing-pages-and-malicious-software
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT department evaluating/migrating between two RMM products on a test machine
  • Managed-service provider that legitimately deploys AnyDesk while a user separately installed HopToDesk for personal use
  • Sysadmin bench machine used to reproduce customer support scenarios with multiple remote tools
  • Security team detonating RMM samples in a sandboxed but Defender-onboarded host
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("it-bench01","soc-detonation01")  // exclude sanctioned RMM-eval hosts
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm neither tool is on the org's approved RMM allowlist and check for a preceding external Teams contact (UC1) or msiexec pull from camorreado.click on the same host. Step 2 (contain): Kill hoptodesk.exe/anydesk.exe, terminate their unattended-access sessions, and isolate the endpoint from the network. Step 3 (hunt): Look for msiexec executing v#.msi from camorreado.click and node.exe beaconing that follows the RMM sessions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("hoptodesk.exe","anydesk.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctTools = dcount(tolower(FileName)), Tools = make_set(FileName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, AccountName
| where DistinctTools >= 2   // HopToDesk + AnyDesk together on one host
| order by FirstSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend Bin = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName,"\\")[-1]))
| where Bin in ("hoptodesk.exe","anydesk.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctTools = dcount(Bin), Tools = make_set(Bin), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), SampleCmd = any(CommandLine) by Computer, SubjectUserName
| where DistinctTools >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\hoptodesk.exe OR *\\HopToDesk.exe OR *\\anydesk.exe OR *\\AnyDesk.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(hoptodesk|anydesk)\.exe$/i
| RmmTool := if(ImageFileName=/hoptodesk\.exe$/i, then="hoptodesk", else="anydesk")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=[count(field=RmmTool, distinct=true, as=distinctTools), collect([RmmTool])])
| distinctTools>=2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as firstSeen, values(Processes.process_name) as tools, dc(Processes.process_name) as toolTypes from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("hoptodesk.exe","anydesk.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where toolTypes>=2   // both HopToDesk AND AnyDesk = campaign's dual-RMM lure
| sort - firstSeen
| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as firstSeen, values(Processes.process_name) as tools, dc(Processes.process_name) as toolTypes from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("hoptodesk.exe","anydesk.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where toolTypes>=2   // both HopToDesk AND AnyDesk = campaign's dual-RMM lure
| sort - firstSeen
Msiexec installing remote EtherRAT loader MSI (v#.msi) from camorreado.click AIInstallation High
Hunts msiexec.exe invoked against a remote MSI hosted on camorreado[.]click (observed as v7.msi from an open directory of v1–v9 installers). This MSI is the EtherRAT loader that fetches a legit Node.js runtime and decrypts embedded payloads — a single-command, high-fidelity execution pivot. Rationale: Pins on the exact delivery domain camorreado[.]click and the v#.msi naming from the open-directory (v1-v9) — msiexec pulling a remote MSI from an attacker domain is inherently rare and the domain string makes FPs near-zero. Cross-checked against: • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2026/06/inside-a-malicious-infrastructure-delivering-etherrat-phishing-pages-and-malicious-software • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/etherrat-dissected-how-a-react2shell-implant-delivers-5-payloads-through-blockchain-c2
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal software-distribution server that happens to name packages v7.msi (mitigated by the camorreado.click requirement, but the regex alone could match)
  • Developer testing a locally hosted MSI over http with a v#.msi filename
  • Legitimate vendor MSI download whose URL coincidentally contains a v-number pattern
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in an onboarded sandbox
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full msiexec command line and confirm the source URL is camorreado.click; check the parent process (was it a browser/RMM session started by the vishing lure?). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block camorreado.click at proxy/DNS, and collect the dropped MSI plus any node.exe artifacts for analysis. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep the estate for other v1–v9 MSI names from camorreado.click and for node.exe spawned by msiexec beaconing to the same domain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "camorreado.click" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)https?://\S*v[1-9]\.msi"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "camorreado.click" or CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)https?://\S*v[1-9]\.msi"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint DNS/network egress to EtherRAT delivery & C2 domain camorreado.click AICommand & Control High
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to camorreado[.]click — the EtherRAT loader-download and campaign C2 domain. Catches both the MSI/Node.js pull and subsequent beaconing regardless of which process (msiexec, node.exe, browser) drives the connection, complementing the msiexec process pivot. Rationale: camorreado[.]click is the article's single confirmed network IOC (corroborated by Malwarebytes' infrastructure write-up); a domain match is a clean pure-IOC detection and the Defender query surfaces the initiating process (expect msiexec.exe or node.exe) for immediate triage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2026/06/inside-a-malicious-infrastructure-delivering-etherrat-phishing-pages-and-malicious-software
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/URL-detonation appliance or analyst sandbox resolving the IOC on purpose
  • Web proxy or DNS-security product pre-resolving flagged domains for categorization
  • Newly-registered lookalike domain reused for benign parking after takedown
  • SOC tooling that pings known-bad domains for availability monitoring
Suppression filter
| where ClientIP !in ("10.10.20.5")  // exclude the URL-detonation sandbox resolver
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process (node.exe from a temp path or msiexec = high concern) and the requesting host/user. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole/block camorreado.click at DNS and proxy, isolate any host with a successful connection, and preserve node.exe + dropped payloads. Step 3 (hunt): Look for the follow-on EtherRAT behaviour — node.exe polling public Ethereum RPC endpoints for its C2 URL — and correlate back to the originating Teams vishing session and RMM installs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "camorreado.click"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name =~ "camorreado.click" or Name endswith ".camorreado.click"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)

SecurityEvent

External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.

Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`

// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
// Article-specific bespoke detection — Fake IT support calls on Microsoft Teams push EtherRAT malware
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("node.js", "v7.msi"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FileName in~ ("node.js", "v7.msi"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Iran-Linked Hackers Use New Cavern C2 Framework to Target Israeli Organizations
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-52691", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2025-9316", "CVE-2025-34291", "CVE-2025-54068", "CVE-2026-55200", "CVE-2026-46817")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

16-Year-Old Linux KVM Flaw Lets Guest VMs Escape to Host on Intel and AMD x86 Systems

The Hacker News
2026-07-06 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A use-after-free bug in Linux's KVM hypervisor can be triggered from a guest virtual machine to corrupt the shadow-page state of the host kernel that runs it. Dubbed 'Januscape' and tracked as&nbsp;CVE-2026-53359, the flaw sits in the shadow MMU code that KVM shares across both Intel and AMD. The public proof-of-concept panics the host; the researcher claims that a separate, unreleased exploit

Suspicious Linux kernel module load from world-writable path (Januscape PoC delivery) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the concrete prerequisite of the CVE-2026-53359 public PoC: a guest (or host) loads a loadable kernel module staged in a non-standard, user-writable directory (/tmp, /dev/shm, /home, /var/tmp) rather than the package-managed /lib/modules tree. The Januscape exploit ships as a .ko that races the shadow-MMU reuse path, so an insmod/finit_module of an out-of-tree module immediately before a host crash is the highest-fidelity host-observable signal available. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete exploit mechanic — the PoC is delivered as a loadable kernel module and needs guest root to insmod it — combined with the universal fact that legitimate modules load from /lib/modules, so a .ko in /tmp or /dev/shm is anomalous. Cross-checked against the researcher's PoC repo (github.com/V4bel/Januscape) and cvefeed.io. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/V4bel/Januscape • https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53359 • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019f386a-6d40-72d9-bd81-e9d9c31c4b92
ATT&CKT1611 T1547.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DKMS rebuilding an out-of-tree driver (NVIDIA, VirtualBox, ZFS) into a staging dir before install
  • Developer testing a self-compiled kernel module from a home/build directory
  • CI/CD kernel module test harness loading .ko artifacts from /tmp
  • Security tooling or eBPF/kernel agents side-loading modules during install
  • Container/nested-virt lab automation deliberately insmod'ing test modules
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dkms","dpkg","rpm","apt","yum","dnf") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/lib/dkms/","nvidia","virtualbox","vboxdrv","zfs","spl"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: On the flagged host, capture the full module path and hash (modinfo <path>, sha256sum), the loading user (confirm root/uid change), and check `dmesg`/journalctl for a KVM oops or taint flag (T/O) within ±5 min of the load. 2) CONTAIN: If the module is unsigned, unrecognized, and the host is a multi-tenant KVM hypervisor, isolate the guest, snapshot for forensics, and disable nested virtualization on the host (kvm_intel.nested=0 / kvm_amd.nested=0) as an emergency mitigation. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same user/host for prior .ko drops, check whether the host kernel predates the fixed stable builds (7.1.3, 6.18.38, 6.12.95, 6.6.144, 6.1.177, 5.15.211, 5.10.260 or a distro backport of commit 81ccda30b4e8), and review all co-tenant guests on the same physical host for the same module hash.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("insmod","modprobe","kmod")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".ko"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/home/","/var/tmp/","/run/user/")
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "/lib/modules/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("insmod","modprobe","finit_module","init_module")
| where SyslogMessage has ".ko"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/home/","/var/tmp/","/run/user/")
| where SyslogMessage !has "/lib/modules/"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Linux Kernel Module Loaded From World-Writable Path (Januscape PoC Delivery)
id: 5c3f9e2a-6b1d-4a7e-9c84-2f1b0d7e4a63
description: Detects insmod/modprobe/kmod loading a .ko kernel module staged in a user-writable directory rather than /lib/modules, matching the CVE-2026-53359 Januscape PoC delivery.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/16-year-old-linux-kvm-flaw-lets-guest.html

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_bin:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/insmod'
      - '/modprobe'
      - '/kmod'
    CommandLine|contains: '.ko'
  selection_path:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/tmp/'
      - '/dev/shm/'
      - '/home/'
      - '/var/tmp/'
      - '/run/user/'
  filter_pkg:
    CommandLine|contains: '/lib/modules/'
  condition: selection_bin and selection_path and not filter_pkg
level: medium
source:linux.auditd (@process.name:insmod OR @process.name:modprobe OR @process.name:kmod) @process.command_line:*.ko* (@process.command_line:*/tmp/* OR @process.command_line:*/dev/shm/* OR @process.command_line:*/home/* OR @process.command_line:*/var/tmp/*) NOT @process.command_line:*/lib/modules/*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(insmod|modprobe|kmod)$/i
| regex("\\.ko", field=CommandLine)
| regex("/(tmp|dev/shm|home|var/tmp|run/user)/", field=CommandLine)
| NOT regex("/lib/modules/", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

KVM host kernel panic / shadow-MMU BUG referencing kvm_mmu_get_child_sp (Januscape trigger) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the observable end-state of the public CVE-2026-53359 PoC: the host kernel notices its corrupted shadow-page records and self-panics, emitting a BUG/Oops/GPF in the KVM shadow-MMU code. On a multi-tenant hypervisor an unexpected kernel-level crash referencing kvm/mmu symbols is a strong indicator that a guest triggered the use-after-free — this is both the DoS impact and the noisy tell before the withheld code-execution variant. Rationale: Anchors on the exact patched function named in the article (kvm_mmu_get_child_sp) plus the article's explicit outcome — 'a guest can knock over the whole host' via a reliable panic. Kernel crashes referencing kvm/mmu on a hypervisor are rare and high-signal. Confirmed against Mallory.ai and cvefeed.io write-ups describing the shadow-MMU UAF and host panic. Cross-checked against: • https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53359 • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019f386a-6d40-72d9-bd81-e9d9c31c4b92 • https://securityonline.info/januscape-kvm-escape-cve-2026-53359-poc/
ATT&CKT1611 T1499.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine hardware fault (bad RAM/ECC) causing a kernel Oops in KVM code paths
  • Buggy out-of-tree driver or unrelated KVM regression panic after a kernel upgrade
  • Nested-virt stress/QA testing that legitimately crashes lab hypervisors
  • Live-migration or hotplug bugs unrelated to CVE-2026-53359 hitting the MMU path
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full crash stack from the host (journalctl -k, /var/log/kern.log, kdump vmcore if configured) and confirm the backtrace includes shadow-MMU frames (kvm_mmu_get_child_sp, FNAME(fetch), mmu_page). Note which guests were running and whether nested virt is enabled. 2) CONTAIN: Treat the physical host as compromised-pending-investigation; migrate/quarantine surviving tenant guests, and disable nested virtualization host-wide (kvm_intel.nested=0 / kvm_amd.nested=0) until patched. 3) HUNT: Correlate the panic timestamp with UC1 (suspicious .ko load) on any co-resident guest, verify the host kernel is below the fixed stable builds or lacks commit 81ccda30b4e8, and expedite patching of every other hypervisor on the same kernel branch.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Facility in~ ("kern","kernel") or ProcessName =~ "kernel"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("kvm_mmu_get_child_sp","kvm_mmu","FNAME(fetch)","__kvm_mmu")
    or (SyslogMessage has "kvm" and SyslogMessage has_any ("kernel BUG","BUG:","Oops","kernel panic","general protection fault","unable to handle kernel"))
| summarize CrashLines = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Sample = make_set(SyslogMessage, 20) by Computer
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.syslog (kvm_mmu_get_child_sp OR (kvm AND ("kernel BUG" OR Oops OR "kernel panic" OR "general protection fault")))
APPLICATION
index=* sourcetype=linux_secure OR sourcetype=syslog OR sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog ("kvm_mmu_get_child_sp" OR "kvm_mmu" OR "FNAME(fetch)" OR (("kvm") AND ("kernel BUG" OR "BUG:" OR "Oops" OR "kernel panic" OR "general protection fault" OR "unable to handle"))) | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(_raw) as sample by host | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Unpatched KVM hosts exposed to Januscape (CVE-2026-53359) — asset exposure AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces the attack surface for CVE-2026-53359 by listing managed x86 Linux hosts that vulnerability management flags as affected. Because distributions backport the one-line fix under different package versions (the article warns not to trust `uname -r` alone), a CVE-keyed inventory query is the cleanest way to prioritize which multi-tenant hypervisors need commit 81ccda30b4e8 before an attacker rents a guest on one. Rationale: Uses the concrete CVE id (CVE-2026-53359) and the article's operational warning that backport version numbers differ per distro, so a scanner/CVE-keyed lookup beats manual kernel-version comparison. AlmaLinux git commits (backports 'ahead of RHEL') confirm distros are shipping the fix under bespoke package builds, validating the CVE-keyed approach. Cross-checked against: • https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53359 • https://git.almalinux.org/rpms/kernel/commit/9d9b973c723a06d2062f5c6ff31f6d4bc3ceb55e
ATT&CKT1611
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched via distro backport but TVM catalog lags in re-scoring the CVE (stale finding)
  • Non-hypervisor Linux endpoint flagged for the kernel CVE but with nested virt / /dev/kvm not actually exposed to untrusted guests (lower real risk)
  • Desktop/CI Linux boxes that carry a vulnerable kernel but never host untrusted tenants
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each returned host, confirm role (is it a multi-tenant KVM hypervisor?) and whether nested virtualization is exposed (`cat /sys/module/kvm_intel/parameters/nested` or `.../kvm_amd/parameters/nested`) — only nested-enabled hosts serving untrusted guests are high-priority. 2) CONTAIN: For high-priority hosts that cannot be patched immediately, set kvm_intel.nested=0 / kvm_amd.nested=0 to remove the attack path, and on RHEL-like distros verify /dev/kvm is not world-writable (0666) to cut the LPE variant. 3) HUNT: Confirm the running kernel actually includes commit 81ccda30b4e8 via the package changelog (not uname -r), then feed patched hosts back to close the finding and schedule reboots for the fixed stable builds.

| project DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, OSDistribution, OSVersion, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cilium Envoy admin socket abuse: TLS secret / config disclosure via admin.sock (CVE-2026-49445) · [LLM] Cilium Envoy admin socket abuse: destructive DoS via /quitquitquit /drain_listeners (CVE-2026-49445)
Cilium Envoy admin socket abuse: TLS secret / config disclosure via admin.sock (CVE-2026-49445) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a local process on a Kubernetes node reading sensitive Envoy admin endpoints (/certs, /config_dump, /clusters) over the world-accessible Cilium Envoy admin.sock. Only cilium-agent/cilium-envoy should ever touch this socket, so any curl/wget/socat/python/nc process referencing it plus a read endpoint is anomalous and indicates exploitation of the mode-0777 socket. Rationale: Anchored on the concrete artifacts corroboration surfaced: the world-accessible socket is admin.sock (mode fixed to 0660 in PR #44512) and the article's 'Exposing TLS secrets' maps precisely to Envoy's /certs and /config_dump admin endpoints (Envoy admin docs). Excluding cilium-* binaries makes non-cilium access to this socket high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44512 • https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/operations/admin.html • https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/security/network/proxy/envoy/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005 T1613
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cilium/Isovalent support engineer running `cilium-sysdump` or manual curl against admin.sock during troubleshooting
  • Custom Prometheus exporter or monitoring wrapper script scraping /stats or /config_dump for observability
  • Platform team debugging L7 policy by dumping Envoy config on a node
  • CI/e2e test harness that exercises the admin interface
  • SRE gathering diagnostics via a non-cilium helper script that shells out to curl
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-sysdump", "cilium-dbg", "cilium-health", "cilium-bugtool"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the acting process, its parent, and the user/UID. Confirm it is NOT cilium-agent/cilium-envoy and not a sanctioned sysdump/monitoring job. Capture which endpoint was hit — /certs and /config_dump mean TLS material and full mesh config may be disclosed. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the node, rotate any TLS secrets/SDS certs served by Envoy on that node, and confirm Cilium is upgraded to a patched build (v1.17.14 / v1.18.8 / v1.19.2) so admin.sock is mode 0660. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host/UID for other admin.sock access, for destructive endpoint hits (/quitquitquit, /drain_listeners), for lateral movement from the identity, and search other nodes for the same process ancestry.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/certs", "config_dump", "/clusters", "server_info", "/stats", "/listeners", "/runtime")
| where FileName !in~ ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy", "cilium")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/certs", "config_dump", "/clusters", "server_info", "/stats", "/listeners", "/runtime")
| where ActingProcessName !has "cilium"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-agent" and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-envoy"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cilium Envoy admin socket abuse: destructive DoS via /quitquitquit /drain_listeners (CVE-2026-49445) AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts when a local process invokes disruptive Envoy admin operations over the world-accessible Cilium admin.sock — /quitquitquit (terminate Envoy), /drain_listeners, /healthcheck/fail, /reset_counters. These directly implement the article's 'disrupting traffic' and 'terminating the Envoy process' impacts and have no legitimate manual use against the Cilium-managed Envoy. Rationale: The article explicitly lists 'Disrupting traffic in the cluster' and 'Terminating the Envoy process' as impacts; Envoy admin docs confirm /quitquitquit terminates the process and /drain_listeners + /healthcheck/fail disrupt serving. These are irreversible operational actions no legitimate operator issues against the Cilium-managed Envoy, making this alertable at high confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44512 • https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/operations/admin.html • https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/security/network/proxy/envoy/
ATT&CKT1489 T1499
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator manually draining a node for maintenance who scripts /drain_listeners against the Cilium Envoy instead of using the node-drain workflow
  • Chaos-engineering / resilience test intentionally failing Envoy healthchecks
  • Support engineer restarting a wedged Envoy via /quitquitquit during an incident
  • Custom automation that resets Envoy stat counters via /reset_counters before a benchmark
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-sysdump", "cilium-dbg", "cilium-bugtool"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Correlate the process/user/UID with any approved change or maintenance window; check whether Envoy on the node restarted or dropped L7 traffic immediately after (cilium-agent logs, pod readiness flaps). 2) CONTAIN: Cordon/isolate the node, restore Envoy (cilium-agent will respawn it) and verify L7 policy enforcement resumed, then ensure the cluster is upgraded to a patched Cilium (v1.17.14 / v1.18.8 / v1.19.2). 3) HUNT: Look for prior read abuse of the same admin.sock (/certs, /config_dump) from the same identity, repeated destructive calls across multiple nodes (coordinated DoS), and the initial access vector that placed the attacker on the node.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("quitquitquit", "drain_listeners", "healthcheck/fail", "reset_counters")
| where FileName !in~ ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy", "cilium")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("quitquitquit", "drain_listeners", "healthcheck/fail", "reset_counters")
| where ActingProcessName !has "cilium"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-agent" and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-envoy"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Twig SSTI markers in request-controlled fields against Craft/Formie public forms AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests carrying Twig template syntax ({{ }}, {% %}) in the User-Agent, Referer, or query string reaching a Craft CMS site running Formie. CVE-2026-52889 copies these request-derived Hidden-field defaults straight into Craft's Twig render layer, so Twig markers in these fields are the earliest observable of exploitation of a public form. Rationale: Uses the exact request-derived input surface named in the advisory (User Agent, Referer, Current URL, Query Parameter) and Twig delimiters {{ / {% (plus URL-encoded %7b%7b). Web-request telemetry only exists in Sentinel W3CIISLog / Splunk Web DM; Defender AH, Datadog standard sources, Falcon FDR and CloudWatch do not carry HTTP request headers, so those queries are intentionally empty. Cross-checked against the sibling Formie SSTI advisory CVE-2026-45697 and the Craft SSTI advisory GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-565m-g33j-jq96 • https://dailycve.com/craft-cms-formie-plugin-twig-injection-via-hidden-field-cve-2026-45697-critical/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw
ATT&CKT1190 T1221
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web vulnerability scanners (Burp, Nuclei, Acunetix) sending {{7*7}} SSTI probes
  • Client-side JS frameworks (AngularJS/Vue/Mustache) passing {{ }} template strings in query params
  • Marketing/analytics referrers containing mustache placeholders like {{campaign}}
  • Bug-bounty researchers testing the public form
  • URLs carrying JSON blobs with doubled braces
Suppression filter
| where scStatus == 200 and csUriStem !contains "/api/" and csUserAgent !has_any ("AngularJS","Vue")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP in the window; confirm the target csUriStem is a page that renders a Formie form and whether scStatus==200 (server processed the payload vs 404/403). Decode the payload from UA/query/cookie. 2) Contain: if the payload contains RCE gadgets or scStatus 200 on a form page, block the source IP at the WAF and confirm Formie is on 3.1.27+; if not, apply the workaround (remove request-derived Hidden-field defaults) immediately. 3) Hunt: pivot to endpoint telemetry on the web host for php/w3wp spawning shells (UC3) and review the same source IP for gadget strings (UC2).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem !endswith ".js" and csUriStem !endswith ".css" and csUriStem !endswith ".png" and csUriStem !endswith ".woff2"
| where csUriQuery contains "%7b%7b" or csUriQuery contains "{{" or csUriQuery contains "%7b%25" or csUriQuery contains "{%"
     or csUserAgent contains "{{" or csUserAgent contains "{%" or csUserAgent contains "_self.env"
     or csReferer contains "{{" or csReferer contains "{%"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, csReferer, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Active Twig RCE gadget strings in Craft/Formie HTTP request inputs AIExploitation High
High-fidelity detection for Twig-to-PHP RCE gadgets (_self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback / getFilter / craft.app) delivered via the request-controlled Hidden-field defaults exploited by CVE-2026-52889. Unlike generic {{ }} probing, these tokens are unambiguous command-execution attempts. Rationale: Anchors on the documented Twig RCE gadget chain _self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback + getFilter and Craft's exposed craft.app object — these strings virtually never appear in benign traffic, so this warrants alerting. Web-request headers/query are only available in Sentinel/Splunk web logs; Defender/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch do not carry them. Gadget syntax corroborated via PayloadsAllTheThings PHP SSTI and the Craft SSTI advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-565m-g33j-jq96 • https://swisskyrepo.github.io/PayloadsAllTheThings/Server%20Side%20Template%20Injection/PHP/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw
ATT&CKT1190 T1221 T1059
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentest/red-team validating CVE-2026-52889 post-patch
  • Vulnerability scanner with a Twig-specific SSTI plugin
  • WAF that replays blocked payloads into a downstream access log
  • Security-training or CTF traffic against a staging Craft instance
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("<authorized_scanner_ip_placeholder_removed>") and csUserAgent !has_any ("Nuclei","nuclei","Burp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the full payload from csUriQuery/csUserAgent/csReferer, identify the command inside getFilter()/filter('system'), and check scStatus + the response size for signs the command executed. Confirm the source IP is not an authorized scanner. 2) Contain: block the source IP, take the affected web node out of the pool if RCE is likely, and force-upgrade Formie to 3.1.27+ (or remove request-derived Hidden-field defaults). 3) Hunt: on the web host, run UC3 for php/w3wp child shells, review new files in web roots (webshell drop) and outbound connections from the PHP worker, and search all web logs for the same source IP and gadget tokens over a wider window.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriQuery has_any ("registerUndefinedFilterCallback","registerUndefinedFunctionCallback","getFilter","_self.env","craft.app")
     or csUserAgent has_any ("registerUndefinedFilterCallback","registerUndefinedFunctionCallback","getFilter","_self.env","craft.app")
     or csReferer has_any ("registerUndefinedFilterCallback","getFilter","_self.env")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, csReferer, scStatus

Craft/PHP/IIS web worker spawning a command shell (Formie SSTI RCE outcome) AIExploitation High
Detects the PHP FastCGI, php-fpm, or IIS worker process backing a Craft CMS site spawning a command interpreter or recon LOLBin — the post-exploitation footprint of a successful Twig SSTI RCE via CVE-2026-52889. A web worker launching cmd/powershell/sh is not normal Craft behaviour. Rationale: Anchors on the specific web-tier parents of a Craft/PHP deployment (php-cgi.exe, php-fpm, w3wp.exe backing IIS+FastCGI, nginx/httpd) spawning shells/recon LOLBins — the concrete execution outcome of the Twig system()/exec gadget the advisory warns can lead to RCE. Purely endpoint telemetry, so no web-log or CloudWatch query. Not covered by generic Office-spawn-script or encoded-PS rules. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-565m-g33j-jq96 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-94rc-cqvm-m4pw
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin running Craft console commands (php craft resave/queue/run) that legitimately shell out
  • Image-processing plugins (ImageMagick/GD) invoked by php calling system utilities
  • Deployment/build steps (composer, npm) executed under the web-service account
  • Monitoring/backup agents launched by the web worker
  • Scheduled Craft queue jobs spawning curl for outbound webhooks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "craft" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("queue/run","resave","gc","migrate")) and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and the parent InitiatingProcessCommandLine — a shell running whoami/id/net/certutil under the web-service account with no interactive admin session is high-signal; correlate the timestamp with UC1/UC2 web-log hits from the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the web host, kill the child process, and revoke/rotate any credentials accessible to the web-service account; confirm Formie is patched to 3.1.27+. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by the php/w3wp worker (webshells), outbound connections from the worker process, new local accounts or scheduled tasks, and repeat the process-tree hunt across all other Craft/Formie web nodes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-cgi.exe","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-cgi.exe","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Threat Actors Probe Gitea Docker Flaw CVE-2026-20896 13 Days After Disclosure

The Hacker News
2026-07-06 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors have been observed attempting to exploit a recently patched critical security flaw in Gitea Docker images, according to Sysdig. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-20896 (CVSS score: 9.8), a vulnerability that stems from the DevOps platform trusting the "X-WEBAUTH-USER" header from any source IP address, effectively allowing an unauthenticated internet client to get elevated

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Gitea CVE-2026-20896 probe source IP 159.26.98.241 (ProtonVPN) contact · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Gitea CVE-2026-20896 auth bypass: X-WEBAUTH-USER header from untrusted source · [LLM] Vulnerable Gitea (≤1.26.2) exposed to CVE-2026-20896
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Gitea CVE-2026-20896 auth bypass: X-WEBAUTH-USER header from untrusted source AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to a Gitea instance carrying the X-WEBAUTH-USER header from any non-loopback / non-trusted-proxy source IP. This is the exact single-header exploit for CVE-2026-20896, where the Docker image's REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES=* default lets any client impersonate any user (admin, gitea_admin) with no password or token. Rationale: Anchors on the literal exploit primitive named in the article and GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4: the X-WEBAUTH-USER header. Defender/Falcon left empty because EDR endpoint telemetry does not capture HTTP request headers; this detection lives in web/proxy/WAF logs. The loopback-exclusion in Sentinel keeps the legitimate trusted-proxy path (127.0.0.0/8) quiet. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/security/advisories/GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4 • https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.26.3-and-1.26.4/ • https://hivesecurity.gitlab.io/blog/gitea-forgejo-nine-cves-1263-security-release-2026/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-20896
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate reverse-proxy auth (Authelia, oauth2-proxy, Cloudflare Access) genuinely injecting X-WEBAUTH-USER from the trusted loopback/proxy IP
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, internal pentest) sending the header as an exploit check
  • Load balancer or uptime health checks replaying a stored request template that includes the header
  • Internal admin testing/validating the reverse-proxy authentication configuration after patching
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "127.0.0.0/8"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full request — note the SourceIP, the X-WEBAUTH-USER value (admin/gitea_admin = high risk), and whether the request bypassed the proxy (direct hit on the container port). Confirm the Gitea build is ≤1.26.2. Step 2 (contain): If the source is external/untrusted, block the IP at the WAF/firewall, force-expire active Gitea sessions, and either set REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.0/8,::1/128 or upgrade to 1.26.3+. Step 3 (hunt): Review Gitea audit logs for admin actions (new SSH keys, tokens, webhooks, repo clones) tied to that session; enumerate all repos accessed since first probe; rotate any secrets/tokens the impersonated account could read.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestContext has "X-WEBAUTH-USER" or Message has "X-WEBAUTH-USER"
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "127.0.0.0/8"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestContext, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gitea CVE-2026-20896 probe source IP 159.26.98.241 (ProtonVPN) contact AIReconnaissance Medium
Alerts on any network connection to/from 159.26.98.241, the ProtonVPN egress IP Sysdig observed making the first in-the-wild probe against internet-facing Gitea instances for CVE-2026-20896. Scoped to Gitea/web-facing hosts. Rationale: Uses the single network IOC the article provides (159.26.98.241). Confidence held at Medium because it is a shared ProtonVPN egress cited only by Sysdig/THN and may be reused by benign users or rotate — hence the host-scoping and analyst-verify runbook rather than auto-block. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threat-actors-probe-gitea-docker-flaw.html • https://dailysecurityreview.com/resources/gitea-cve-2026-20896-auth-bypass-exploited-via-one-http-header/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote developer or admin browsing to Gitea over ProtonVPN sharing the same egress IP
  • Security researchers or benign internet-wide scanners (Shodan, Censys) transiting the same VPN pool
  • VPN egress reassignment over time making the IOC stale and matching unrelated traffic
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox infrastructure that replays IOCs for validation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the local asset is an internet-facing Gitea/web host and check the connection direction and port — inbound to the Gitea HTTP port is the concern. Correlate with UC1 (X-WEBAUTH-USER header) for the same timeframe. Step 2 (contain): If tied to a header-bypass request or admin action, block 159.26.98.241 at the perimeter and expire Gitea sessions; if it is only a benign browse from a known dev, allowlist the user, not the IP. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep 30 days of firewall/WAF logs for the same IP against all web assets, and check whether the same source attempted other Gitea endpoints (/admin, /api/v1/admin).

Vulnerable Gitea (≤1.26.2) exposed to CVE-2026-20896 AIExploitation High
Exposure hunt surfacing hosts running Gitea versions vulnerable to CVE-2026-20896 (fixed in 1.26.3) via vulnerability-management telemetry, so they can be patched or reconfigured before the header bypass is weaponized against them. Rationale: Pins the concrete CVE id (CVE-2026-20896) and patched build (1.26.3) from the article and Gitea's release blog into vulnerability-management datamodels. Sigma/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because VM inventory is not expressible on their event-shaped log sources. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/security/advisories/GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4 • https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.26.3-and-1.26.4/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-20896
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Isolated dev/test Gitea instances not reachable from the internet (still worth patching but lower priority)
  • TVM keying on container image digest may mis-map or miss containerized Gitea deployments
  • Forgejo forks mis-attributed as Gitea by the scanner
  • Instances already reconfigured with REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.0/8,::1/128 but not yet version-upgraded (mitigated, still flagged)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each flagged host confirm the exact Gitea build and whether reverse-proxy auth (ENABLE_REVERSE_PROXY_AUTHENTICATION) is enabled and internet-exposed. Step 2 (contain): Upgrade to Gitea 1.26.3+ (or 1.26.4); as an interim mitigation set REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES to 127.0.0.0/8,::1/128 and disable reverse-proxy auth if not required. Step 3 (hunt): For any host that was exposed, retro-hunt web/proxy logs for X-WEBAUTH-USER (UC1) and contact from 159.26.98.241 (UC2) to determine if it was probed or compromised before patching.

| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
